The report provides a historical analysis of foreign affairs funding appropriations in the United States Congress from 1994 to 2020. Prior to 2008, Congress allocated funds for the Department of State and international broadcasting through different appropriations bills. However, since 2008, these funds have been consolidated under the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs (SFOPS) appropriations.

SFOPS appropriations consist of State Department Operations, Foreign Operations, various international commissions, and International Broadcasting. State Department Operations include Embassy Security, Construction, and Maintenance, and Education and Cultural Affairs, among others. Foreign Operations funding is typically about twice as much as State Operations funding and includes USAID administration expenses, bilateral economic assistance, international security assistance, multilateral assistance, and export assistance.

The report highlights that since FY1995, Congress has passed foreign affairs funding on time in freestanding bills only once, and it has included funding within an omnibus, consolidated, or full-year continuing resolution 21 of the past 25 years. Many foreign policy experts argue that stand-alone appropriations legislation would allow for more rigorous debate on specific foreign policy activities and improve the ability to fund new programs or cancel existing ones.

The report also discusses the importance of authorization bills, which not only authorize funding for obligation and expenditure but also provide a forum for more rigorous debate on foreign affairs and foreign aid policies. However, in recent years, Congress has not enacted a foreign relations and foreign aid authorization bill.

The report concludes by discussing the impact of the Budget Control Act of 2011 and the Bipartisan Budget Acts of 2015 and 2018 on foreign affairs funding levels. The BCA has put downward pressure on SFOPS enduring/base funds while encouraging a migration of funds for ongoing activities into OCO-designated accounts. However, the 2018 BBA has had the opposite effect, allowing lawmakers to shift OCO funding back into enduring/base accounts.

answers: Congress currently appropriates most foreign affairs funding through annual Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs (SFOPS) appropriations. Prior to FY2008, however, Congress provided funding for the Department of State, international broadcasting, and related programs within the Commerce, Justice, State, the Judiciary, and Related Agencies appropriations. In those years, Congress separately appropriated funding for the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) and foreign aid within the Foreign Operations, Export Financing, and Related Programs appropriations. The 110th Congress aligned the two foreign affairs appropriations into the SFOPS legislation. SFOPS appropriations since FY2001 have included enduring appropriations (ongoing or base funding), emergency supplemental appropriations, and Overseas Contingency Operations (OCO) appropriations. Total SFOPS funding levels in both current and constant dollars show a general upward trend, with FY2004 as the peak largely as a result of emergency supplemental appropriations for Iraq Relief and Reconstruction Funds. When adjusted for inflation, annual foreign affairs appropriations have yet to surpass the FY2004 peak. The Budget Control Act (BCA) of 2011 and the Bipartisan Budget Acts (BBA) of 2015 and 2018 appear to have had an impact on both enduring and OCO funding levels. The legislative history of SFOPS appropriations shows that nearly all foreign affairs appropriations measures within the past 25 years were passed within omnibus, consolidated, or full-year continuing resolutions, rather than in stand-alone bills. Moreover, many appropriations were passed after the start of the new fiscal year, at times more than half way into the new fiscal year. In many fiscal years, SFOPS appropriations included emergency supplemental funding or, since FY2012, OCO funding.
